questions: What information about itself may an APP entity need to give an individual when collecting their personal information?
Which details concerning the collecting entity are among the matters an APP entity must notify or ensure the individual is aware of?
answer: The identity and contact details of the APP entity are among the matters that must be notified or made known, as far as reasonable in the circumstances. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence: (a) the identity and contact details of the APP entity;

statement: If an APP entity collects personal information from someone other than the individual, or the individual may not be aware of the collection, the matters include the fact of the collection and its circumstances.
questions: When an APP entity collects personal information from a third party rather than the individual, what must it notify or make the individual aware of?
What collection-related matters must an APP entity address if the individual may not know it has collected their personal information?
answer: The matters include the fact that the entity so collects, or has collected, the information and the circumstances of that collection. This applies if the entity collects from someone other than the individual or the individual may not be aware of the collection. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence: the fact that the entity so collects, or has collected, the information and the circumstances of that collection;

statement: If collection is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order, the matters include that fact, including the name of the law or details of the order.
questions: What must an APP entity convey when collection of personal information is required or authorised by an Australian law or court/tribunal order?
If an Australian law or a court or tribunal order requires or authorises collection, what details about it are among the matters an APP entity must notify?
answer: The matters include the fact that the collection is so required or authorised, including the name of the Australian law, or details of the court/tribunal order, that requires or authorises it. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence: the fact that the collection is so required or authorised (including the name of the Australian law, or details of the court/tribunal order, that requires or authorises the collection);

statement: The matters include the purposes for which the APP entity collects the personal information and the main consequences (if any) for the individual if all or some of it is not collected.
questions: What must an APP entity address regarding why it collects personal information and what happens if it is not collected?
Which matters about purposes and consequences of non-collection are among those an APP entity must notify an individual of?
answer: The matters include the purposes for which the entity collects the personal information, and the main consequences (if any) for the individual if all or some of the information is not collected. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence:
(d) the purposes for which the APP entity collects the personal information;
(e) the main consequences (if any) for the individual if all or some of the personal information is not collected by the APP entity;

statement: The matters include any other APP entity, body or person, or types of them, to which the APP entity usually discloses personal information of the kind collected.
questions: What must an APP entity convey about the parties to which it usually discloses the kind of personal information it collects?
Which matter about usual disclosures to other entities, bodies or persons is among those an APP entity must notify an individual of?
answer: The matters include any other APP entity, body or person, or the types of them, to which the entity usually discloses personal information of the kind collected by it. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence: (f) any other APP entity, body or person, or the types of any other APP entities, bodies or persons, to which the APP entity usually discloses personal information of the kind collected by the entity;

statement: The matters include that the APP privacy policy contains information about access and correction, and about how to complain about a breach and how the complaint will be dealt with.
questions: What must an APP entity say about its APP privacy policy when notifying an individual of the collection of personal information?
Which privacy policy content on access, correction and complaints must an APP entity notify or make an individual aware of?
answer: The matters include that the entity's APP privacy policy contains information about how the individual may access and seek correction of their personal information, and how they may complain about a breach of the Australian Privacy Principles or a binding registered APP code and how the entity will deal with the complaint. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence: (g) that the APP privacy policy of the APP entity contains information about how the individual may access the personal information about the individual that is held by the entity and seek the correction of such information;

statement: The matters include whether the entity is likely to disclose the information to overseas recipients and, if so, the countries where they are likely to be located if practicable to specify them.
questions: What must an APP entity convey about likely overseas disclosure of personal information it collects?
When must an APP entity specify the countries of likely overseas recipients when notifying an individual about collection?
answer: The matters include whether the entity is likely to disclose the information to overseas recipients and, if so, the countries in which such recipients are likely to be located, if it is practicable to specify those countries in the notification or otherwise make the individual aware of them. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence: (i) whether the APP entity is likely to disclose the personal information to overseas recipients;

statement: An APP entity need only take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances to notify the individual of, or make the individual aware of, the listed matters, and only those matters that are reasonable in the circumstances.
questions: How far must an APP entity go in notifying an individual about the listed matters when it collects personal information about them?
What qualifies the steps an APP entity must take to notify an individual of, or make them aware of, collection matters?
answer: An APP entity must take only such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances, and must notify or make the individual aware only of those listed matters that are reasonable in the circumstances. [Source: Sch 1, APP 5]
evidence:
the entity must take such steps (if any) as are reasonable in the circumstances:
(a) to notify the individual of such matters referred to in subclause 5.2 as are reasonable in the circumstances

statement: Under APP 6, an APP entity holding personal information collected for a primary purpose must not use or disclose it for a secondary purpose unless an exception applies.
questions: What general restriction applies to an APP entity that holds personal information collected for a particular purpose when it wants to use or disclose it for a different purpose?
Can an APP entity use or disclose personal information for a purpose other than the one it was collected for, and if so, when?
answer: An APP entity must not use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose (another purpose than the primary purpose for which it was collected) unless the individual consented or one of the listed exceptions applies. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence:
the entity must not use or disclose the information for another purpose (the secondary purpose) unless:
(a) the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information; or

statement: The primary purpose is the particular purpose for which the personal information was collected, and the secondary purpose is another purpose.
questions: In the Australian Privacy Principle on use or disclosure, what is meant by the 'primary purpose' of personal information?
How does the Privacy Act define the 'secondary purpose' for which an APP entity may use or disclose personal information?
answer: The primary purpose is the particular purpose for which the personal information was collected, while the secondary purpose is any other purpose for which the entity uses or discloses it. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: that was collected for a particular purpose (the primary purpose), the entity must not use or disclose the information for another purpose (the secondary purpose)

statement: A secondary use or disclosure is permitted where the individual would reasonably expect it and, for sensitive information, the secondary purpose is directly related to the primary purpose.
questions: When can an APP entity use or disclose sensitive information for a secondary purpose on the basis of the individual's reasonable expectation?
What test must a secondary purpose meet for sensitive information to be used or disclosed based on what the individual would reasonably expect?
answer: The individual must reasonably expect the APP entity to use or disclose the information for the secondary purpose, and the secondary purpose must be directly related to the primary purpose. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: (i) if the information is sensitive information—directly related to the primary purpose; or

statement: For non-sensitive information, a secondary use or disclosure within the individual's reasonable expectation is permitted if the secondary purpose is related to the primary purpose.
questions: What relationship must a secondary purpose have to the primary purpose for an APP entity to use or disclose non-sensitive personal information based on reasonable expectation?
When may an APP entity use or disclose personal information that is not sensitive information for a secondary purpose the individual would reasonably expect?
answer: The individual must reasonably expect the use or disclosure for the secondary purpose, and the secondary purpose must be related to the primary purpose. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: (ii) if the information is not sensitive information—related to the primary purpose; or

statement: A secondary use or disclosure is permitted where a permitted general situation exists, or, for an organisation, where a permitted health situation exists.
questions: Which situations, apart from consent and legal authority, permit an APP entity to use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose on general or health grounds?
Is an organisation permitted to use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose where a permitted health situation exists?
answer: Use or disclosure is permitted where a permitted general situation exists in relation to it; and where the APP entity is an organisation, where a permitted health situation exists. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence:
(c) a permitted general situation exists in relation to the use or disclosure of the information by the APP entity; or
(d) the APP entity is an organisation and a permitted health situation exists

statement: A secondary use or disclosure is permitted where the APP entity reasonably believes it is reasonably necessary for enforcement related activities conducted by or on behalf of an enforcement body.
questions: What enforcement-related ground allows an APP entity to use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose?
What must an APP entity reasonably believe in order to use or disclose personal information for an enforcement body's activities?
answer: The APP entity must reasonably believe that the use or disclosure is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: the APP entity reasonably believes that the use or disclosure of the information is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body.

statement: An agency that is not an enforcement body may disclose biometric information or templates to an enforcement body if the disclosure accords with the Commissioner's guidelines.
questions: Under what conditions may an agency that is not an enforcement body disclose biometric information or biometric templates to an enforcement body?
Which guidelines must be followed when an agency discloses biometric templates to an enforcement body under the use or disclosure principle?
answer: The agency must not be an enforcement body, the information must be biometric information or biometric templates, the recipient must be an enforcement body, and the disclosure must be conducted in accordance with the Commissioner's guidelines made for that purpose. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence:
(a) the agency is not an enforcement body; and
(b) the information is biometric information or biometric templates; and
(c) the recipient of the information is an enforcement body; and

statement: An organisation to which the permitted health situation collection rule applied must take reasonable steps to de-identify the information before disclosing it.
questions: What must an organisation do before disclosing personal information that it collected under the permitted health situation research provision?
Is an organisation required to de-identify personal information before disclosure where the health-related collection provision applied to its collection?
answer: The organisation must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure the information is de-identified before disclosing it under the use or disclosure principle's permitted grounds. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the information is de-identified before the entity discloses it

statement: An APP entity that uses or discloses personal information for enforcement related activities must make a written note of the use or disclosure.
questions: What record must an APP entity make when it uses or discloses personal information because it reasonably believes this is necessary for enforcement related activities?
Is an APP entity required to document a use or disclosure made for enforcement related activities?
answer: The APP entity must make a written note of the use or disclosure. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: If an APP entity uses or discloses personal information in accordance with paragraph 6.2(e), the entity must make a written note of the use or disclosure.

statement: An APP entity may use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose if the individual has consented to the use or disclosure.
questions: Does an individual's consent allow an APP entity to use or disclose personal information for a purpose other than the one it was collected for?
What effect does an individual's consent have on the prohibition against an APP entity using or disclosing personal information for a secondary purpose?
answer: An APP entity may use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose where the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: (a) the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information; or

statement: A secondary use or disclosure is permitted where it is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order.
questions: Is an APP entity allowed to use or disclose personal information for a secondary purpose when an Australian law or a court or tribunal order requires or authorises it?
What happens to the restriction on secondary use or disclosure when an Australian law or court/tribunal order requires or authorises the use or disclosure?
answer: A secondary use or disclosure is permitted where it is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence: (b) the use or disclosure of the information is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order; or

statement: APP 6 does not apply to an organisation's use or disclosure of personal information for direct marketing or of government related identifiers.
questions: Which uses or disclosures by an organisation fall outside the use and disclosure principle in the Privacy Act's Australian Privacy Principles?
Does the principle restricting use or disclosure for secondary purposes apply to an organisation using personal information for direct marketing or disclosing government related identifiers?
answer: The principle does not apply to the use or disclosure by an organisation of personal information for the purpose of direct marketing, or of government related identifiers. [Source: Sch 1, APP 6]
evidence:
6.7 This principle does not apply to the use or disclosure by an organisation of:
(a) personal information for the purpose of direct marketing; or
(b) government related identifiers.

statement: An organisation that holds personal information about an individual must not use or disclose it for the purpose of direct marketing, unless an exception applies.
questions: What is the general rule on using or disclosing held personal information for direct marketing under the Australian Privacy Principles?
Under the Privacy Act, may an organisation that holds an individual's personal information use or disclose it for direct marketing by default?
answer: If an organisation holds personal information about an individual, it must not use or disclose the information for the purpose of direct marketing, subject to the stated exceptions. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: If an organisation holds personal information about an individual, the organisation must not use or disclose the information for the purpose of direct marketing.

statement: An organisation may use or disclose non-sensitive personal information for direct marketing if it collected the information from the individual, the individual would reasonably expect that use, it provides a simple opt-out means, and the individual has not opted out.
questions: Under what conditions may an organisation use or disclose non-sensitive personal information it collected from the individual for direct marketing?
What four conditions must be met for an organisation to direct market using non-sensitive personal information collected from the individual themselves?
answer: The organisation must have collected the information from the individual, the individual must reasonably expect the use or disclosure for that purpose, the organisation must provide a simple means to easily request not to receive direct marketing communications, and the individual must not have made such a request. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence:
(a) the organisation collected the information from the individual; and
(b) the individual would reasonably expect the organisation to use or disclose the information for that purpose;

statement: Where the individual would not reasonably expect the direct marketing use, or the information was collected from someone else, non-sensitive information may be used for direct marketing only if the individual consented or obtaining consent is impracticable.
questions: When information was collected from someone other than the individual, what consent-related condition allows an organisation to use non-sensitive personal information for direct marketing?
What alternative to individual consent allows direct marketing use of non-sensitive personal information where the individual would not reasonably expect it?
answer: Either the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information for direct marketing, or it is impracticable to obtain that consent. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence:
(i) the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information for that purpose; or
(ii) it is impracticable to obtain that consent;

statement: The second non-sensitive exception applies where the organisation collected the information from the individual and the individual would not reasonably expect the use for direct marketing, or collected it from someone other than the individual.
questions: From whom or in what circumstances must non-sensitive personal information have been collected for the exception covering unexpected or third-party sourced information to apply?
Which collection circumstances are covered by the exception allowing direct marketing with non-sensitive information where consent or impracticability is shown?
answer: The organisation collected the information either from the individual where the individual would not reasonably expect the use or disclosure for direct marketing, or from someone other than the individual. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence:
(i) the individual and the individual would not reasonably expect the organisation to use or disclose the information for that purpose; or
(ii) someone other than the individual;

statement: Under the second non-sensitive exception, in each direct marketing communication the organisation must include a prominent statement that the individual may request not to receive such communications, or otherwise draw the individual's attention to that fact.
questions: What must an organisation include in each direct marketing communication when relying on the exception for unexpected or third-party collected non-sensitive information?
How must an organisation inform an individual of the right to opt out in each direct marketing communication under the consent or impracticability exception?
answer: In each direct marketing communication, the organisation must include a prominent statement that the individual may make an opt-out request, or otherwise draw the individual's attention to that fact. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence:
(i) the organisation includes a prominent statement that the individual may make such a request; or
(ii) the organisation otherwise draws the individual's attention to the fact that the individual may make such a request;

statement: An organisation may use or disclose sensitive information for direct marketing if the individual has consented to that use or disclosure for that purpose.
questions: What is required for an organisation to use or disclose sensitive information about an individual for direct marketing?
Under the Privacy Act, when may sensitive information be used or disclosed for direct marketing by an organisation?
answer: An organisation may use or disclose sensitive information about an individual for direct marketing if the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information for that purpose. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: an organisation may use or disclose sensitive information about an individual for the purpose of direct marketing if the individual has consented to the use or disclosure of the information for that purpose.

statement: A contracted service provider for a Commonwealth contract may use or disclose personal information for direct marketing if it collected the information to meet an obligation under the contract and the use or disclosure is necessary to meet such an obligation.
questions: When may an organisation that is a contracted service provider for a Commonwealth contract use or disclose personal information for direct marketing?
What conditions apply to the contracted service provider exception permitting direct marketing?
answer: The organisation must be a contracted service provider for a Commonwealth contract, must have collected the information for the purpose of meeting (directly or indirectly) an obligation under the contract, and the use or disclosure must be necessary to meet such an obligation. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence:
(a) the organisation is a contracted service provider for a Commonwealth contract; and
(b) the organisation collected the information for the purpose of meeting (directly or indirectly) an obligation under the contract;

statement: Where an organisation uses or discloses personal information for its own direct marketing, the individual may request not to receive direct marketing communications from it.
questions: What may an individual request when an organisation uses their personal information for its own direct marketing?
Which request can an individual make to an organisation that uses or discloses their information for the purpose of direct marketing by that organisation?
answer: The individual may request not to receive direct marketing communications from the first organisation. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: (c) if paragraph (a) applies—request not to receive direct marketing communications from the first organisation;

statement: Where an organisation uses or discloses personal information to facilitate direct marketing by other organisations, the individual may request that it not use or disclose the information for that purpose.
questions: What may an individual request when an organisation uses or discloses their information to facilitate other organisations' direct marketing?
Which request is available to an individual whose information is used to facilitate direct marketing by other organisations?
answer: The individual may request the organisation not to use or disclose the information for the purpose of facilitating direct marketing by other organisations. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: (d) if paragraph (b) applies—request the organisation not to use or disclose the information for the purpose referred to in that paragraph;

statement: An individual whose information is used for direct marketing or its facilitation may request the organisation to provide its source of the information.
questions: What may an individual ask an organisation about the origin of their personal information used for direct marketing?
Can an individual request that an organisation identify where it obtained their information when it is used for direct marketing?
answer: The individual may request the first organisation to provide its source of the information. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: (e) request the first organisation to provide its source of the information.

statement: An organisation must not charge an individual for making a direct marketing-related request or for giving effect to it.
questions: May an organisation charge an individual for making or giving effect to a request not to receive direct marketing or for the source of information?
What is the rule on fees for individuals' requests under the direct marketing principle?
answer: The organisation must not charge the individual for the making of, or to give effect to, the request. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: the first organisation must not charge the individual for the making of, or to give effect to, the request

statement: An organisation must give effect to an opt-out or non-use/disclosure request within a reasonable period after the request is made.
questions: Within what time must an organisation give effect to a request not to receive direct marketing communications?
By when must an organisation act on an individual's request not to use or disclose their information for facilitating others' direct marketing?
answer: The organisation must give effect to the request within a reasonable period after the request is made. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: the first organisation must give effect to the request within a reasonable period after the request is made

statement: An organisation must notify the individual of its source of the information within a reasonable period after a request, unless impracticable or unreasonable.
questions: When must an organisation tell an individual the source of their information after a request for it?
In what circumstances may an organisation decline to notify an individual of its source of their information for direct marketing?
answer: The organisation must, within a reasonable period after the request is made, notify the individual of its source unless it is impracticable or unreasonable to do so. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: the organisation must, within a reasonable period after the request is made, notify the individual of its source unless it is impracticable or unreasonable to do so.

statement: The direct marketing principle does not apply to the extent that the Do Not Call Register Act 2006, the Spam Act 2003, Division 5 of Part 7B of the Interactive Gambling Act 2001, or other prescribed Commonwealth or external Territory laws apply.
questions: Which other legislation displaces the direct marketing principle to the extent it applies?
To what extent does the direct marketing principle not apply because of other laws such as the Spam Act?
answer: The principle does not apply to the extent that Division 5 of Part 7B of the Interactive Gambling Act 2001, the Do Not Call Register Act 2006, the Spam Act 2003, or any other prescribed Commonwealth Act or external Territory law applies. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]

statement: Under the non-sensitive information exceptions for direct marketing, the organisation must provide a simple means by which the individual may easily request not to receive direct marketing communications, and the individual must not have made such a request.
questions: What opt-out conditions must be satisfied for an organisation to use non-sensitive personal information for direct marketing under the exceptions?
What must an organisation provide, and what must the individual not have done, for the non-sensitive information direct marketing exceptions to apply?
answer: The organisation must provide a simple means by which the individual may easily request not to receive direct marketing communications from it, and the individual must not have made such a request to the organisation. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence:
the organisation provides a simple means by which the individual may easily request not to receive direct marketing communications from the organisation; and
(d) the individual has not made such a request to the organisation.

statement: A note to the direct marketing principle says that an act or practice of an agency may be treated as an act or practice of an organisation.
questions: Under the Privacy Act's direct marketing principle, can the act or practice of an agency be treated as that of an organisation?
What does the note to the direct marketing principle say about how an agency's act or practice may be treated in relation to an organisation?
answer: The note states that an act or practice of an agency may be treated as an act or practice of an organisation. [Source: Sch 1, APP 7]
evidence: Note: An act or practice of an agency may be treated as an act or practice of an organisation, see section 7A.

statement: Before disclosing personal information to an overseas recipient, an APP entity must take reasonable steps to ensure the recipient does not breach the APPs (other than APP 1) in relation to the information.
questions: What must an APP entity do before it discloses personal information about an individual to a recipient outside Australia?
Before an APP entity sends personal information to an overseas recipient, what steps does the Privacy Act require it to take?
answer: The APP entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the overseas recipient does not breach the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 1) in relation to the information. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: the entity must take such steps as are reasonable in the circumstances to ensure that the overseas recipient does not breach the Australian Privacy Principles (other than Australian Privacy Principle 1) in relation to the information.

statement: The overseas recipient is a person who is not in Australia or an external Territory and who is not the APP entity or the individual.
questions: Who counts as an "overseas recipient" for the purposes of the cross-border disclosure principle?
How does the Privacy Act define the overseas recipient to whom an APP entity discloses personal information?
answer: An overseas recipient is a person to whom the entity discloses personal information who is not in Australia or an external Territory, and who is not the APP entity itself or the individual concerned. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]

statement: The reasonable steps requirement does not apply if the entity reasonably believes the recipient is subject to a law or binding scheme protecting the information in a way at least substantially similar to the APPs and the individual can access enforcement mechanisms.
questions: When does the requirement to take reasonable steps before overseas disclosure not apply because of the legal protections that govern the recipient?
What belief about the overseas recipient's legal environment exempts an APP entity from the reasonable steps requirement for cross-border disclosure?
answer: It does not apply if the entity reasonably believes that the recipient is subject to a law or binding scheme protecting the information in a way that, overall, is at least substantially similar to the APPs, and that there are mechanisms the individual can access to enforce that protection. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: the recipient of the information is subject to a law, or binding scheme, that has the effect of protecting the information in a way that, overall, is at least substantially similar to the way in which the Australian Privacy Principles protect the information; and

statement: The exception based on a similar law or binding scheme also requires that there are mechanisms the individual can access to enforce the protection.
questions: Besides the recipient being subject to a substantially similar law or binding scheme, what else must an APP entity reasonably believe to rely on that exception to the overseas disclosure requirement?
What enforcement-related belief is required for the similar-law exception to cross-border disclosure obligations?
answer: The entity must also reasonably believe that there are mechanisms that the individual can access to take action to enforce the protection of the law or binding scheme. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: there are mechanisms that the individual can access to take action to enforce that protection of the law or binding scheme; or

statement: The reasonable steps requirement does not apply if the individual consents to the overseas disclosure after the entity expressly informs them that consent means the requirement will not apply.
questions: How can an individual's consent exempt an APP entity from the reasonable steps requirement for overseas disclosure?
What must an APP entity tell an individual for their consent to remove the reasonable steps requirement for cross-border disclosure?
answer: The entity must expressly inform the individual that if they consent to the disclosure, the reasonable steps requirement will not apply, and after being so informed the individual must consent to the disclosure. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: the entity expressly informs the individual that if he or she consents to the disclosure of the information, subclause 8.1 will not apply to the disclosure;

statement: A permitted general situation exempts the disclosure from the reasonable steps requirement, except the situations in items 4 or 5 of the table in section 16A(1).
questions: Which permitted general situations are excluded from exempting an APP entity from the reasonable steps requirement for overseas disclosure?
How do permitted general situations affect the reasonable steps requirement for cross-border disclosure?
answer: The requirement does not apply where a permitted general situation exists in relation to the disclosure, other than the situations referred to in item 4 or 5 of the table in subsection 16A(1). [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: a permitted general situation (other than the situation referred to in item 4 or 5 of the table in subsection 16A(1)) exists in relation to the disclosure of the information by the APP entity;

statement: An agency is exempt from the reasonable steps requirement if the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an international agreement relating to information sharing to which Australia is a party.
questions: When is an agency exempt from the reasonable steps requirement for overseas disclosure because of an international agreement?
What type of international agreement can make an agency's overseas disclosure exempt from the reasonable steps requirement?
answer: Where the entity is an agency and the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an international agreement relating to information sharing to which Australia is a party. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: the entity is an agency and the disclosure of the information is required or authorised by or under an international agreement relating to information sharing to which Australia is a party;

statement: An agency is exempt where it reasonably believes the disclosure is reasonably necessary for enforcement related activities by or on behalf of an enforcement body and the recipient performs similar functions or exercises similar powers to an enforcement body.
questions: What conditions let an agency disclose personal information overseas for enforcement related activities without the reasonable steps requirement?
When is an agency's overseas disclosure to a body similar to an enforcement body exempt from the reasonable steps requirement?
answer: The agency must reasonably believe the disclosure is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by or on behalf of an enforcement body, and the recipient must be a body that performs functions or exercises powers similar to those of an enforcement body. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: the entity reasonably believes that the disclosure of the information is reasonably necessary for one or more enforcement related activities conducted by, or on behalf of, an enforcement body;

statement: Subclause 8.3 applies if the recipient is subject to the laws of a country prescribed by the regulations or is a participant in a binding scheme prescribed by the regulations.
questions: What kinds of recipients bring the prescribed country or binding scheme exception into play for overseas disclosure?
Under the Privacy Act, when does the prescribed country or scheme provision apply to an APP entity's disclosure to an overseas recipient?
answer: It applies if the recipient is subject to the laws of a country prescribed by the regulations, or is a participant in a binding scheme prescribed by the regulations. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence:
(i) subject to the laws of a country that is prescribed by the regulations; or
(ii) a participant in a binding scheme that is prescribed by the regulations; and

statement: If a country or binding scheme is prescribed subject to conditions, those conditions must be satisfied for the prescribed-country or scheme provision to apply.
questions: What must be satisfied when a country or binding scheme is prescribed subject to conditions for overseas disclosure purposes?
Where regulations prescribe a country or binding scheme with conditions, what is required for the exemption to apply to an APP entity's overseas disclosure?
answer: The conditions attached to the prescription of the country or binding scheme must be satisfied. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: if the country or binding scheme is prescribed subject to conditions—those conditions are satisfied.

statement: Under section 16C, an act or practice of the overseas recipient is in certain circumstances taken to have been done by the APP entity and to be a breach of the APPs.
questions: In certain circumstances, how can an overseas recipient's act or practice be treated under the Privacy Act in relation to the disclosing APP entity?
What consequence can follow for an APP entity from an overseas recipient's acts or practices relating to disclosed personal information?
answer: In certain circumstances, an act done or practice engaged in by the overseas recipient is taken to have been done or engaged in by the APP entity and to be a breach of the Australian Privacy Principles. [Source: Sch 1, APP 8]
evidence: In certain circumstances, an act done, or a practice engaged in, by the overseas recipient is taken, under section 16C, to have been done, or engaged in, by the APP entity and to be a breach of the Australian Privacy Principles.

statement: The requirement to take reasonable steps before disclosing personal information overseas does not apply if the disclosure is required or authorised by or under an Australian law or a court/tribunal order.
questions: Under the Australian Privacy Principles, when does the requirement to take reasonable steps before an overseas disclosure not apply because of an Australian law or a court or tribunal order?
